title: Control Room Layout: 8 Smart Design Rules for Safer Shifts
text:
Design

 Control Room Layout: 8 Smart Design Rules for Safer Shifts

 Operators spend twelve hour shifts watching a plant they rarely see, so the room around them shapes every decision they make. A well planned layout keeps screens readable, teams talking and equipment safe, even during the worst upset.

 
 ISO 11064 
 Console Arrangement 
 Video Wall Sightlines 
 Rack Room 
 Blast Resistance 
 




 A control room is far more than a hall full of screens. This guide explains how ISO 11064, console arrangement, sightlines, rack rooms, siting, HVAC and lighting come together in a practical control room layout for process plants.


 
 Hello everyone, today we are going to learn how a control room layout is planned, from ISO 11064 principles and console arrangement to video wall sightlines, rack rooms, blast resistance, HVAC and lighting.


 
 
 

 What Is Control Room Layout?


 Control room layout is the planned arrangement of operator consoles, displays, support rooms and building services so that operators can monitor and control the process safely and comfortably. In a modern plant it is the home of the distributed control system operator stations, the safety system interfaces and the communication tools.


 The layout covers several levels: the site location of the building, the grouping of rooms, the position of each console and finally the dimensions of each workstation. Mistakes at any level are expensive to correct once the plant is running.


 
 
 Image credit: Motilde . Photo courtesy of Motilde, shown here for educational reference. 
 

 Mary Ann Lane and Peggy Hewitt of BAW Architecture write in Control Global that the size and quantity of consoles should dictate the size of the room. In other words, you design from the operator outward, not from the building inward.


 
 
 Advertisement 


 
 


 ISO 11064 and the Seven Parts


 ISO 11064 is the main international standard for the ergonomic design of control centres, and Control Global notes that its first parts were published in 2000. Motilde lists its seven parts as design principles, arrangement of control suites, control room layout, workstation layout and dimensions, displays and controls, environmental requirements and evaluation.


 
 Part 1 Principles for the design of control centres

 Part 2 Arrangement of control suites

 Part 3 Control room layout

 Part 4 Workstation layout and dimensions

 Part 5 Displays and controls

 Part 6 Environmental requirements

 Part 7 Principles for evaluation




 The UK Health and Safety Executive points to ISO 11064 as guidance for new control rooms and for upgrades where problems are known. It also refers to EEMUA 201 for practical guidance on process control desks and screens.


 Do You Know?
 Control Global cites a 2002 Shell study by Harrie Rensink that estimated up to 15 percent capital savings when control rooms are designed correctly the first time. Rework after commissioning is far more costly.



 Console Arrangement in a Control Room Layout


 The console arrangement decides who can see whom, who can see the shared displays and how far people walk during an upset. Each operator position normally holds several HMI screens, a keyboard, a phone and radio, and sometimes a hardwired panel.


 
 Linear Row
 Consoles side by side facing one wall.
 Best for: small rooms with one or two operators
 Simple 

 Arc or Horseshoe
 Consoles on a curve facing a shared video wall.
 Best for: central control rooms with several units
 Popular 

 Cluster or Pod
 Small groups around a shared task or unit.
 Best for: large sites with separate areas
 Team focus 

 Raised Supervisor Desk
 Shift supervisor placed behind and slightly above the operators.
 Best for: multi unit control rooms
 Overview 




 Hardwired emergency push buttons and the emergency stop panel must be within easy reach of the responsible operator. Older plants also keep a mimic panel , but most new designs replace it with a large overview display.


 Quick Tip
 Build a full size mock up of one console with cardboard or foam and let real operators sit at it. Reach, sightline and leg room problems show up in minutes.



 Sightlines and Video Wall Readability


 Every operator must be able to read the shared overview display from the normal seated position, without standing or leaning. Readability depends on the character height and the viewing distance, which together give the visual angle in arc minutes.


 Extron, citing the videowall book by Robert Simpson, gives 10 arc minutes as the bare minimum for legible text and 15 to 20 arc minutes for the furthest viewer as a safer rule. A good control room layout checks this for the operator seated furthest from the wall.


 
 Character height h = D × tan(θ ÷ 60) 

D = viewing distance in mm, θ = visual angle in arc minutes
The angle ÷ 60 is in degrees

Example: D = 5 m = 5000 mm, θ = 20 arc minutes
θ ÷ 60 = 0.3333 degrees, tan(0.3333 degrees) = 0.005818
 h = 5000 × 0.005818 = 29.1 mm

 Second Worked Example for a Larger Room


 In a larger central room, the furthest operator sits 8 m from the video wall. At 20 arc minutes the minimum character height is 8000 × 0.005818, which is about 46.5 mm.
